column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The entry dates her arrival to 48 CE; the article gives no year of arrival (its lead gives her dates as 32-189). Not used. The article's lead says the Ayodhya memorial was built in 2020, while its memorial section says it was inaugurated in 2001 and expanded from 2018; only the 2018 foundation stone is given. The article's count of the children (12; two Heo, eight Kim sons, two daughters, then seven more sons named as monks) does not add up; only the first part is used.
The entry dates his death c. 534 and the battle to 531; the article gives his death as 532 and the attack as 531 or 532. No year is given for either in the text.
The article gives 530 BC without c.; the entry has c. 530 BCE. No date repeated.
The article calls Alain's son Jean I of Albret in its history but lists him as Jean II in its list of lords; no numeral is used.

The entry says Mingrelia accepted Russian protection in 1803; the article says the Dadiani accepted Russian sovereignty in 1802. No year given. The article gives the family's earliest records as 1046, before the entry's start date (13th century); left out. The article says Levan III abdicated in 1691, but its own list has Levan III 1661-1681 and Levan IV 1681-1691; the prince is not named.

The entry says she was made queen in 1689; the article says she was queen from 1690 (its titles list also gives 1690), though its narrative puts the appointment shortly after her 1689 promotion. No year is given for her queenship. The entry says she rose through the ranks from 1686; the article's narrative gives 1686 for the sugwon rank, its titles list 23 January 1687. No year given for that rank.

The entry dates the Nicaraguan landfall to 16 November 2020; the article's meteorological history puts it at about 03:40 UTC on 17 November, while its Nicaragua section says 16 November. No date given for the landfall. The article gives the distance from Eta's landfall as 14 mi in one place and 15 mi in another; written as a few miles.

The article gives Ozolua's reign as 1483-1514, which conflicts with Esigie's reign from 1504 (entry and article). Ozolua's dates are left out. The article tells the oracle story twice: once the oracle advises Idia herself, once her parents. Worded without saying who made the cuts.

The article gives his birth as 1892 or 1893 in the lead and 1893 in the text; the entry has 1892. No year given. The article's lead gives his death as 25 March 1976 in Tehran, its text the summer of 1976 at his home (after his move to Urmia). Only the year is given.

The entry says he was captured by a Tang army under Li Jing; the article says his own men, Ashina Sunishi and Ashina Nishu, captured him and handed him to Li Daozong and Zhang Baoxiang. Worded as 'soon taken'. The entry dates his reign from 620; the article gives no year.

SKIPPED: The article has about 360 words, most of them already in the entry (grass bridges, the road system, chasqui, mit'a repairs, the Q'iswa Chaka); what is left (ichu grass, Huamán Poma's drawing, the Apurímac bridge and Thornton Wilder's novel) is under 200 words.
SKIPPED: The article has about 260 words in all; a longer text of 260 words would only restate every sentence of it.

The entry says the institute was revived in 1859; the article says its activities resumed in 1836 as The Egyptian Society, which moved to Alexandria and became the Institut Égyptien in 1859. The 1836 date is left out.
The entry ends his reign in June 1360; the article gives his overthrow and death as 24 June or 13 July 1360. No date given in the text.

The article gives the mound's size as both a 60 m circumference and a 60 m diameter; the figure was left out. The article dates the inscribed silver bowl both to the 6th-5th century BCE and to approximately the 4th century BCE; no date for the bowl is given. The article says the sex of the skeleton is indeterminate; the entry's 'young warrior' was not repeated or contradicted.
The article spells the kingdom Karague; the text names it only by its place west of Lake Victoria, to avoid a spelling the entry (Karagwe) does not use.

The article calls the state the Belarusian Democratic Republic and his office 'president of the Rada'; the entry says 'first chairman of the Rada of the Belarusian People's Republic'. The text avoids both forms of the title.

DISAGREEMENT: the entry dates his death to 846; the article dates his assassination to 841 (citing the Shoku Nihon Koki, Ennin's diary and the National History Compilation Committee). The text gives no year of death. The article gives a birth year of 787, which the entry does not; left out with the death year. The article calls him Chang Pogo; the text uses the entry's spelling.
The entry calls him minister of development in 1833; the article says he became Home Minister that year. The text does not name his 1833 office.
The entry says he was overthrown by the army; the article says he resigned when Riché was proclaimed president. Both are compatible; the text says he resigned.

The article gives several inconsistent dates in its late-history section (Mittasena 275-301, the same as Mahasena's 273-301; the Dhammaruci sect overrunning the stupa in the 'mid 2nd century AD', before it was built); these were left out. Parakramabahu's restored height is given both as 210 feet and as the present c. 70 m; only the present height is used.

The article dates the Eastern Wu as 229-280 in the lead and 222-280 in its list of the Six Dynasties, and the Southern Dynasties to 420-552 though it lists the Chen to 589; no dates for the dynasties are given.
The article's lead gives her dates as c. 865-898 but its body says she died in December 897, as the entry has it; only the body's date is used.
The article is short and mostly a list of works; the text draws on that list. Ottobeuren is dated 1737-1766 in the article.
The article's account of the Fort Warren performance of 12 May 1861 matches the entry's date and was not repeated.

The entry says he introduced the Lutheran Reformation in 1538; the article says the area became Lutheran with his accession and that he joined the Schmalkaldic League in 1538. The text gives no date for the Reformation itself. The article misspells 'Loardship' of Cottbus; written as Lordship.

The entry says he received Beirut after its recovery in 1197; the article says only that he exchanged the constableship for Beirut sometime before 1205. No date is given for the grant. The article calls him 'a principled man' and the natural leader of the barons; not repeated as a judgement.
The entry names the Laguatan; the article calls the same tribe the Leuathae. Both names appear on the page.

The article dates San Martín's landing at Pisco to September 1819, after the Riego coup of January 1820; the date is left out. The article's text breaks off before the Battle of Ayacucho, which the entry describes; nothing about it was added.

The article says he was created a baronet on 20 June 1911 but tells it after his resignation of March 1912; the baronetcy is left out. The article dates his founding of the Ministry of Health and Tourism to 1901 but tells it within his first premiership; left out.

SKIPPED: the article has little substance on the county's history (population, an old ginkgo tree, administrative divisions, two notable people, modern honours) and nothing on the State of Ju or the Neolithic sites the entry describes

The article gives Tebandeke's reign as c. 1704 - c. 1724 and Ndawula's as c. 1724 - c. 1734; these dates are left out as approximate. The article lists Muwenda Mutebi II as reigning from 1993 to the present; not included to avoid present-tense claims.

The article calls it the first structural temple built in South India; the entry says the oldest structural temple in the city. Not repeated. The article's suggestion that it may be built of a geopolymer is left out.

The article dates the style from Middle Minoan IA (c. 2100 BCE) to Late Minoan IA (c. 1450 BCE), and its phases MM IA c. 2100-1925, MM IB c. 1925-1875, MM II c. 1875-1750, MM III c. 1750-1700 BCE; the entry's dates are c. 2000-1700 BCE, so no absolute dates are given in the text. The article does not mention the Kamares cave or Mount Ida.
The entry speaks of the Mahakam in East Kalimantan; the article mentions the upper Kayan, the middle Kapuas and the Mahakam, consistent.

The article says he was deputy director of the National Museum in Warsaw 'since 1939', oddly placed in the post-war section; left out. The article calls the bust's site the Museum of Egyptian Antiquities in Cairo.
The article spells the brother as Malla Bek, Muhammad Malla Beg Khan and Mallya Khan; Seyid Khan is called a son of Mallya Khan. The article does not give his birth year (entry: 1829).
The article gives his dates as 734-761 and says he took poison probably in 761; consistent with the entry's d. c. 761. Khurshid's flight to Daylam and his poisoning are in the entry and not repeated.
The article dates the assassination of King Liao to 515 BC while the reign runs from 514 BC; the year of the killing is left out. Zuili, named in the entry, is not in the article.

The article does not give the date of the Union of Lublin; the entry's 1569 is not repeated. The article says the Mieszko II crisis followed 1031 and that Bolesław II regained the crown in 1076 with Pope Gregory VII's support.
The 2019 restoration and its king (Niokhobaye Fatou Diène Diouf, apparently living) are mentioned only as a dated fact, without the king's name.
The article says only that Mary, Queen of Scots was once held prisoner on the island; the entry's 1567-1568 is not repeated.

The article gives his birth year as 1180 without c.; the entry has c. 1180. The year is not repeated. The article says the inquisition covered Thuringia and Hesse and the Upper Rhineland; the entry says Rhineland and Hesse. Consistent.

The article says the Armed Forces Day campaign honours 'the foundation of the Korean Liberation Army in 1941', contradicting its own 1940; no year is given there. The article spells the commander's name both Chi Ch'ŏngch'ŏn and Ji, and Kim Gu also as Kim Ku.
The article calls the NKVD the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs.

The article gives conflicting dates for the charter: after the Battle of Krina (1235), Niane's 'in 1236', and Nesbitt's 'created in 1222'. No year is given in the text. Edict counts: Article 1 speaks of five clans of marabouts, while the article's summary speaks of four clans of guardians of the faith; the number is left out.

The article gives his death as 20 March 1604 in the lead and 19 April 1604 in the Death section; only the year is given. The article says he became a Christian at 38; the age is left out. Buzen province, named in the entry, is not in the article.

The chronicles disagree on his birth: Zata gives 21 July 1030, Hmannan implies 1041. Only Zata's date is given, attributed. The entry names the rebel Nga Yaman Kan; the article spells him Yamankan. The article's spelling is used. The article says the chronicles disagree on whether Saw Lu died in 1082/83 or 1084; that point is left out.

The article gives the commonly estimated death toll as 10,000 to 40,000; the entry says about 10,000 to over 30,000. No total figure is given in the text. The article dates the start of martial law and the military response to 24 January but also says martial law followed the rebellion; worded without a date.

The article says Abu Bakr ibn Umar succeeded his 'brother' Yahya ibn Ibrahim; this kinship looks like a slip (confusion with Yahya ibn Umar) and is left out. The article names the present chief of the tribe, a living politician; left out. Thin article (about 440 words, part of it present-day); text kept short.
The article says the copies were made on Taizong's request and the original was 'said to have been' buried with him; the entry already gives the burial, so it is not repeated.

The entry gives his death as c. 773; the article gives c. 775 and 'almost certainly before 776'. No year of death is given in the text. The article says Saint Ludger rebuilt the church 'a few years later', placed after the destruction of 882, which is unclear in sequence; left out.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words, mostly a museum list and plans; it gives c. 1600 and the mid-19th century where the entry has the 17th century and the 1830s
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words and adds little to the entry; it dates Mstislavl to 1393 where the entry has about 1390

The entry says he led the 552 expedition to Hispania. The article says Jordanes, writing in 551, names him as its leader and J. B. Bury accepts it, while James O'Donnell argues he was in Constantinople and had no time for the campaign. Left out of the text to avoid contradicting the entry; the dispute might be noted on the entry itself. The article gives his Gaul tenure as 510-536 but also says he was back in Italy by 534; worded 'for more than two decades'.
The list of jiedushi does not say Liu Yan founded Southern Han; the text only puts the dates side by side.
SKIPPED: article has about 260 words, mostly transport, shops and climate; its history is one sentence
The entry says it was the longest bridge in Asia when completed; the article says 'one of the longest'. Left out. The article calls Daydé & Pillé architects; written as 'designed by'.

The entry says he fought in the Vendée revolt; the article describes his service in the Chouannerie. The text uses the article's term without contradicting the entry. The article says he went into exile in Spain after 1830, the entry says he went into exile; fine.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words and adds little beyond the naming and two definitions of the language border
The article's own lead gives 'originally Ngô Tuấn' but its body sets out the Ngô and Quách theories; both are given, attributed.
The article dates the Banate of Macsó to 1247; the entry says around 1254. No date is given in the text.
Louis of Orléans was pardoned when Charles VIII came of age; left out for length.

The article spells the ruler Tirumala Nayaka; the entry has Thirumalai Nayak. Same dates, so no conflict. Article: Meenakshi committed suicide by poison in 1739 according to traditional accounts; left out.

The article gives his birth as 23 December 1730 (the entry says c. 1730) and contradicts itself on his death: 13 February 1794 in the lead, 12 February 1794 in the death section. No day printed. Dalrymple's remark that he kept the imperial family starved left out (the article misspells the name); Keeney's verdict of 'the greatest man in India' left out as praise.

The entry dates the formation to December 1941; the article says the graduates of the training school officially formed the First Independent Force in March 1942. The March 1942 date is left out. Casualty figures disputed (MPAJA claimed 5,500 Japanese killed; Japanese gave 600); left out.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: etymology of the title and one court custom; too little for a longer text
The entry dates the Tamoio peace to 1563; the article gives no year, so none is printed.

The article gives his birth as 2 August 1828; the entry's dates say 1827. No birth year printed. The article's statement that he began a revolutionary movement in August 1866 with the Pact of Ostend after two years of exile is self-contradictory; left out.

The article says Trajan renamed an existing city, Parthenopolis; the entry says he founded it. The earlier name and city are left out. The entry's events of 376-377 are not in the article; nothing added on them.
The article says he was consecrated bishop by Charles Borromeo on 17 February 1566, after resigning Cassano in 1561; left out as unclear.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance once its list of towns is set aside; it names the lordships differently from the entry (Badenweiler, Rötteln and Sausenburg)

The article says the Golden Madonna was either commissioned by her or given to her; the entry says commissioned. Not mentioned in the longer text. Her founding of Rellinghausen Abbey is unproven (a forged grave inscription); left out.

The entry says the rising was led by Pieter de Coninck and Jan Breydel; the article does not name Breydel and says de Coninck had fled before 14 May and returned on 23 May. The leadership of the night attack is not stated in the longer text.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; it adds little beyond the entry

The article dates the Medieval Inquisition from 1184 (episcopal) with the Papal Inquisition from the 1230s; the entry defines it as the papal tribunals from the 1230s. The 1184 episcopal inquisition is told as a forerunner.
The article says the Portuguese blockaded the port from 1694 to 1696; left out for length.

The article gives his dates as 1610-1674 in the lead but says he died in 1672; no death year printed. Howorth's claim that the Crimeans slaughtered 30,000 prisoners after Chudnov is left out (a single old source).
The article (Mauduit) also gives 25,000 wounded in the FLN-MNA fighting; left out for length.
The article calls Jobun Michu's nephew and father-in-law at once; only father-in-law is used.
The Union Island uprising named in the entry is not in the article; nothing added on it.
The article treats the civilising mission across many empires; the entry frames it as French. The text keeps France first and the other powers as further uses, which does not contradict the entry.

The article names the Kushano-Sasanian coin legend as Miuro; the entry says Miiro on the coins of the Kushan emperors. Left out of the text. The article's claim that the sun's chariot is 'known as the swastika' and the folk myths of Mithra's birth are not used.
The article dates the building to the third quarter of the 10th century, consistent with the entry's 950s or 960s; neither figure repeated.
The article dates the second Mongol sweep through Anatolia to 1255; the entry has Baiju's second victory in 1256. Left out of the text.

The entry dates the invasions 1297-1306 (their peak); the article covers 1221-1327. The text keeps the peak within the entry's years. Article: Jaran-Manjur army 'led by Ulugh Khan and probably Zafar Khan'; only Ulugh Khan named.

Entry: suppression executed 'over 400 people'. Article: troops killed 439 directly and arrested 354 who were later executed (and elsewhere 'killed more than 400... arrested more than 300'). Death and execution counts left out of the text. Gordon is named in the entry; the article calls him a mixed-race representative of St. Thomas-in-the-East.
The article's paragraph on Thornton v Howe is confused about how the mortmain statutes bore on the case; the text keeps only the holding and that the statutes were in force.
The article says little of the 1933 revolt and the founding of the republic, which the entry covers; it calls him the 'exiled leader' of the republic by 1935.
The entry places Yusuf IV in 1432; the article has Granada recognise Yusuf IV late in 1431 and his execution in 1432. The text gives no date for Yusuf IV's accession.
The article gives his birth as c. 1660 in the lead and c. 1670 in the body; the entry has c. 1660. No birth year in the text.
Article: martyrs were 22 Catholic and 23 Anglican converts, executed 31 January 1885 to 27 January 1887; consistent with the entry, not repeated.
Article dates his reign c. 974-939 BC; the entry gives c. 978-943 BCE. No regnal years in the text. The article's date for Ninurta-kudurri-usur I (c. 983-981 BC) also left out.

The article dates the Karla chaitya dedication to 120 CE and the Junnar inscription to 124 CE (Saka year 46), which assumes the Shaka-era reading; left out, as the period is disputed and the entry says only late 1st or early 2nd century.
Article dates al-Qubavi's translation to 1128 or 1129; the entry says 1128. The text says only 12th century.

Article: died 968 or 969; entry d. 969. No year of death in the text. Entry: ruler of Mosul from 929. Article: his father died in 929, he held only part of the lands, regained Mosul in 930 and 934 and was recognised in late 935. The text gives the course of events without saying when his rule began; editor may judge.
The article dates the party's founding to 27 February 1902, consistent with the entry. Present-day holdings of mayoralties ('currently') left out.
The article names the minister only as M. Marie. The article has under 400 words; the text uses all of its substance not already in the entry and stops there.
Article: born 11 February 1821, died 5 November 1840 (his father's death day); the entry gives d. 1840 and the same day. The death date is not repeated.

The entry calls it a lunar calendar era; the article calls it lunisolar, with an intercalary month. The text says lunisolar, which describes the calendar's months; editor may judge whether this reads as a contradiction.
The entry's description of the Argentine campaigns is consistent with the article (1878-1885); not repeated.

The article makes Oranyan (Oranmiyan) a son of Ogun and the youngest of Oduduwa's grandsons; the entry calls him Oduduwa's youngest son. Left Oranyan out of the text. Left out the Kisra/Mecca origin tradition recorded by Samuel Johnson for length.
The article dates his reign from 732; the entry gives 729 to 761. Left the start of the reign undated in the text.
The article says some followers also worship the deity directly; the entry says people do not worship Olorun directly. Left the point out. Modern pop-culture mentions (songs, Smite, Olodum) left out.

The article gives his death as 7 December 1869 in the lead but 'the night of the 5th' (November) in the body, and its dates for the attack and treatment (8 October, 20 September) are muddled between calendars. Left the days of attack and death out.

The article says that by 1973 the military had ousted the imperial regime (the Derg came to power in 1974); left that framing out. The article gives no year for the OLF's withdrawal from the Transitional Government; the entry says 1992. Not repeated. Left out the 2015 Moyale attack, the 2018 attack in western Oromia and the 2020 Gawa Qanqa killings for length.

The article does not give the year Osberht became king directly (Æthelred's death 'generally placed in 848'; Symeon's 854 as fifth year); the entry says 'from about 849'. Left his accession year out. Ragnar saga material left out as it concerns Ælla.
The article spells the battle Mimigawa; the entry has Mimikawa. Used the article's spelling as it is the same battle. The entry's 'led his clan from 1550' is not in the article; not repeated.
Short article (about 390 words); two sections only.

Toyota genealogy material left out. The article says the line proper ended in 1551 with Yoshinaga, who was not of Ōuchi blood; the entry speaks of the Mōri destroying 'the last of the line' in 1557. Worded as the end of the clan in 1557, as the article also says.
The article's lead says he returned to Spain in 1821; the body says he left on 20 December 1820; the entry implies 1820. Left the year of return out.
The article says 1056 was 'the second year' of the Liao dynasty; this is plainly an error (the dynasty began in the 10th century) and was left out.
The article gives his birth as 29 November (O.S. 17 November) 1853 in the lead and 17 November 1853 in the body; left the day out.

The article dates the tiger reserve both to 1994 and to 2007; left the year out. It also says the tigers were all gone in 2009 and again 'in February 2012'; kept only the June 2009 announcement, which agrees with the entry. Year of declaration (1981, in the entry) is not in the article.

Short article (about 350 words). The article does not date the founding of Luanda (the entry says 1576) and does not mention the wars with Ndongo; it speaks of an alliance under orders for peaceful relations. Neither point contradicted.
The article dates the funeral chariot of the barrows to the 5th century BCE while giving the revised date of barrows 1-5 as 4th-3rd centuries BCE (as the entry has). Left the chariot's date out.

The article gives a meander length of 715 km; the entry says about 790 km. Left the length out. The entry's link to the Republic of West Florida and the Florida Parishes in 1810 is not in the article; not repeated.
The article calls it 'one of the largest' Hindu temple complexes in East Java; the entry says 'the largest'. Size not restated.
The article gives over 1.3 million artifacts; the entry says around a million objects. No figure given in the text.
The article dates the outer wall to c. 1340; the entry says it was added soon after the tower. Kept as 'about 1340'.
Article dates Pharnavaz 299-234 BC (Toumanoff) and 302-236/4 BC in its list; no reign years given to avoid conflict with the entry's 'around 300 BCE'.
The article dates the Illyrian capture to 231 BC; the entry says 230 BCE. No year given for it in the text.
The article is mostly lists of recordings and film uses; the text covers the main ones.
Article dates the Plan 820-830; the entry says c. 820. No date given in the text.
Entry says Rosas went into exile in Britain; not in the article, not repeated.

The article says the relic was acquired during the 14th century in one place and brought to Prato in the 13th century in another, and places the main 'expansion' in the 15th century while dating the bell tower 1356. No date given for the relic's arrival or the enlargement.
The article calls Deodoro da Fonseca a marshal; the entry calls him a general. No rank given in the text.
The entry's statement that the Pshavs supplied warriors to the kings of Kakheti is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article says Quentovic was probably founded in the early 6th century (coins from the 560s) and abandoned probably in the early 11th century (potash glass of the late 11th century); the entry says active from the 7th to the 9th century and gone by the late 10th century. Founding and final abandonment dates left out.
The article places his praetorship in Hispania Ulterior; the entry says Hispania Citerior. Written as 'in Spain'.

The article gives his rule as 1149-1169 in its lead while dating his death to 6 September 1170; the entry says 1149 to 1170. End of reign not stated in the text. The entry's mention of his court's patronage of learning and building is not in the article.

The entry calls Oweynagat a cave of the complex; the souterrain ogham reading follows the article. Inauguration on Rathcroghan Mound is given as a belief ('more than likely' in the article); the O'Conor kings used nearby Carnfree.
The entry says he joined the Third Crusade; the article does not mention it, so it is not repeated here.

Left out: Teja Schwaner's claim to have heard Marley play it in Hamburg in 1976 (the article itself doubts it, and it would sit badly with the entry's 'written c. 1979'). Rolling Stone and New Statesman list placings left out as rankings.

The entry dates him 1519–1544; the article gives his birth as 5 February 1513 and also says he was only 25 when he died (which fits neither). Birth year and age left out. The article adds Gelre to his stadtholderates.
The article is short (about 300 words) and much of it is in the entry already; the text keeps to what the article adds.

The article spells the founder Diether V, the entry Dieter V; the name is left out of the text. The article says 'the state of Rhineland-Palatinate' gave the ruin in 1924 (that state was formed later); written 'the state'.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words (course, three bridge dates, an Ossian line); not enough for 260 words beyond the entry without padding
The entry gives the length as about 50 km; the article says approximately 30 miles (48 km). Length left out. The rise below Aran Fawddwy is not in the article.
The article has the Tummel fall into the Tay 'just below Logierait'; the entry says 'near Ballinluig'. The exact confluence is left out. Loch Faskally (in the entry) is not in the article.

The article's lead says Anthony was in Iran from 1 December 1599 to May 1600 and brought '5000 horses'; both left out as unclear. Its claim that the army reform made the Safavids an equal to the Ottomans is given as 'credited with'.

The article's lead gives 'fl. 865' (from the Fragmentary Annals' eclipse date); the entry says he was earl in the late 9th century. The date is left out. Rollo's identification is already in the entry, so only the French sources' doubt is added.
The article also counts him king of Kakheti 1648–1656. Its account of the 1639–1642 conspiracy is given only in outline.

The entry says the charter was revoked in 1900; the article says it was revoked in 1899 and the territories transferred on 1 January 1900. The revocation year is left out. The article's lead says the territories became the Southern Nigeria Protectorate, its body that they formed both Northern and Southern Nigeria; worded without the split.

De Anda's (2007) view that most victims were killed before being thrown in is said of cenotes in general in the article, so it is left out. The entry's 'pilgrims still visited it at the Spanish conquest' rests on Landa; not repeated.
The article does not date the cession of the Northern Circars or mention the Battle of Udgir; both are in the entry and not repeated.

The article calls Rzayev's film Azerbaijan's first feature film, which is doubtful (perhaps the first after independence); left out. The many recent pop versions (Eurovision singers, Sami Yusuf, Toto Cutugno, Lara Fabian) are left out for length.

The article dates the first wooden bridge c. 1230 (before 1234); the entry says the early thirteenth century. The date is left out. The text of 1608 is O'Neill's flight from Ulster to Rome; only the loss of gold is kept.
Taraori is given in the article as 110 km north of Delhi. The entry says Prithviraj was 'later executed'; the article's 'killed for treason' after a rebellion fits it.

The article is short (about 300 words) and much of it is in the entry; the text adds the parade, Thumelicus, Arminius's death and the name. The article's order puts the residence last though Germanicus died in 19; kept as the article has it, without a date.
The entry spells the wife Stratonice, the article Stratonike; her name is left out of the text. The entry's 'c. 410' end fits the article's 'at least 411'.

The article gives his birthplace as Aleppo 'or in Kuhbanan, Iran, according to some historians'; the entry says Aleppo, so the birthplace is left out. His reply to the sultan, 'I am 104 years old' around 1430, implies a birth about 1326, against the entry's 1330: the age is left out ('pleading his great age'). The article does not say that the sultan became his disciple (the entry does); it tells only the invitation, so nothing on discipleship is said.
The article dates Shah Mahmud's death only as 'the next year' after Shaikh Awais's death in 1374; no year is given in the text.

The entry calls Sherburn a village; the article calls it a town (it does use 'town' for the Civil War garrison, which I kept as the article's wording of the 1640s). The present-day section says only 'civil parish'. Notable residents, media and schools left out.

The article calls him Shi Le's 'distant nephew and adopted brother'; the entry says 'nephew'. Not contradicted: the text gives the actual relationship without the word. The entry dates his rule as emperor from 334; the article says he took 'Regent Heavenly King' in 334, 'Heavenly King' in 337 and emperor only in 349. I stated the titles without calling the 334 title emperor or denying the entry's wording.

The article's lead says the Liao 'would later annex' the Sixteen Prefectures after his rise; the entry says he ceded them. The text does not speak of the cession, so neither version is printed. The rebellion of 936 itself and the Khitan campaign are not in the excerpt given (only the background to it), so they are not told.
